title: API Security Best Practices: A Practical Selection and Implementation Guide
description: An actionable API security checklist covering authentication, authorization, input validation, rate limits, secrets, sensitive data, logging, and continuous testing.
author: Marcus Rivera

sections.title: Inventory and classify API exposure
sections.body: Create an inventory of public, partner, internal, and administrative API endpoints, including versions and owners. Mark which endpoints read or change sensitive data, perform privileged actions, or trigger costly operations. Remove abandoned routes and document supported versions and deprecation dates. Security review should cover the actual deployed surface, including gateway routes and background jobs, rather than only the source code's intended endpoints.

sections.title: Authenticate clients and authorize every request
sections.body: Use an established identity protocol and validate token signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and required scopes. Authentication answers who is calling; authorization must separately determine whether that caller can perform the requested action on the specific object. Check object-level permissions on every read and write, not just at the route level. Avoid trusting user IDs, tenant IDs, roles, or ownership fields supplied by the client without server-side verification.

sections.title: Validate inputs and limit resource use
sections.body: Validate types, lengths, formats, enumerations, and relationships at the API boundary. Use parameterized database operations and safe output handling to reduce injection risks. Apply request-size limits, pagination caps, timeouts, concurrency controls, and rate limits suited to each operation. Expensive exports, search, image processing, and password-reset flows may need stricter quotas than ordinary reads. Return consistent errors without leaking stack traces, secrets, or internal database details.

sections.title: Protect secrets and sensitive data
sections.body: Keep API keys, signing keys, and database credentials in a managed secret store or protected environment configuration, never in source control or client bundles. Rotate credentials on a defined schedule and immediately after suspected exposure. Minimize the personal or confidential data returned by each endpoint, mask sensitive values in logs, and use TLS for data in transit. Define retention and deletion behavior for request logs and exported files.

sections.title: Make browser and service boundaries explicit
sections.body: Configure CORS for the specific origins and methods that need browser access; CORS is not authentication and does not stop non-browser clients. For cookie-based sessions, use appropriate secure cookie settings and CSRF protections for state-changing actions. For service-to-service calls, use distinct identities and narrow permissions rather than a shared organization-wide token. Keep administrative endpoints behind stronger access controls and avoid exposing them through public routing by accident.

sections.title: Test continuously and prepare for incidents
sections.body: Include authorization tests for another user's records, another tenant's resources, expired tokens, missing scopes, malformed input, oversized payloads, and rate-limit behavior. Scan dependencies and deployed configurations, and add regression tests for every confirmed vulnerability. Monitor authentication failures, privilege changes, unusual request rates, and repeated validation failures without recording sensitive payloads. Maintain a response plan for token revocation, key rotation, affected-user notification, and forensic log preservation.

sections.title: Apply safe defaults to errors and responses
sections.body: Use a consistent error structure with a safe public message and a correlation identifier that support staff can use to find the corresponding internal event. Do not return framework exceptions, SQL details, file paths, access tokens, or environment variables to clients. Set response headers and content types deliberately, and ensure that caches do not store personalized or confidential responses for the wrong user. Review logs and traces for sensitive payloads before enabling broad production collection.

sections.title: Prioritize remediation by exposure
sections.body: Rank API findings by exploitability, data sensitivity, reachable attack surface, and business impact rather than treating every scanner result equally. Assign an owner and due date to each accepted risk, and document compensating controls for issues that cannot be fixed immediately. Re-test the deployed endpoint after a change; a passing unit test alone does not prove the gateway, identity policy, and production configuration are correct. Review the inventory whenever a new service or API version is released.
